items.title: The October jobs report is out Friday. Here's everything to expect
items.summary: The Bureau of Labor Statistics releases the October nonfarm payrolls report Friday at 8:30 a.m. ET.
items.body: The U.S. economy isn't expected to have produced much job growth in October, with employers reluctant to hire workers but also not cutting staff amid a shrinking labor force and a growing problem of long-term unemployment. Economists are looking for a meager nonfarm payrolls gain of 59,000, a slight uptick from the 29,000 jobs produced in September, according to the Dow Jones consensus. That result would continue a pattern of sparse growth. But that's kind of OK: The forecast also is that the unemployment rate will hold at a very low 4.2% rate, the product of a climate where a stagnant labor force reduces the need for outsized job increases to keep the jobless level steady. "Long-term, we're not going to need as many jobs added to the economy to have stable employment because we have fewer people who are available to work," said Nicole Bachaud, labor economist at jobs site ZipRecruiter.

items.title: CNBC's experts on whether the AI trade is ending and what investors should do next
items.summary: The big Democratic win on Tuesday is changing the technology investment math.
items.body: Amid a powerful rout in tech stocks, investors told CNBC on Thursday that something may be fundamentally breaking in the AI trade following the big success of Democrats in Tuesday's midterm elections and the threat they try to slow the data center buildout. Democrats are more aggressively anti-data center than Republicans, and Wall Street is quickly redoing its math what any restrictions they implement could mean for the related companies' future growth. "Right now, investors are questioning that $1.2 trillion of capex that we forecast for next year," Peter Boockvar, chief investment officer at One Point BFG Wealth Partners, told CNBC. "Well, maybe that's not going to happen." Boockvar believes this could be the start of the end of the AI trade as we know it.

items.title: Major tech stocks plunge as US midterms add to fears of AI slowdown
items.summary: The market has been reacting to possible tougher scrutiny of data centre construction and the AI industry following the US midterms
items.body: Hundreds of billions of dollars in market value has been wiped from major tech firms in a stock market rout after the US midterm elections sparked concerns of a slowdown in AI development. Following Democratic wins after election campaigns run on slowing AI, shares in firms across the tech and artificial intelligence sectors plummeted. The tech-heavy Nasdaq composite stock index closed down by more than 5.5% to lose an estimated $2.5tn in market capitalisation, according to Dow Jones data, while other key US stock indexes also saw big losses in their worst days since 2025. The sell-off comes on top of broader concerns about whether the huge amounts being spent on AI will pay off.

items.title: Bank of England raises interest rates to 4%, the first increase for more than three years
items.summary: Base rate increases from 3.75% and Bank governor signals another rise in near future to combat rising inflation Analysis: Interest rate rise in midst of cost of living crisis will leave many incredulous The Bank of England has raised interest rates for the first time in three…
items.body: The Bank of England has raised interest rates for the first time in three years and warned of another increase to combat inflationary pressure unleashed by the Iran war. Eight members of the Bank’s monetary policy committee (MPC) voted for the rise, which takes the base rate from 3.75% to 4%. The ninth member, Catherine Mann, preferred a more dramatic half-point increase. The Middle East conflict has pushed oil prices persistently above $100 a barrel in recent months, as hopes have evaporated of a deal that could reopen the strait of Hormuz . As a result, the Bank now expects UK inflation to rise to 4.9% in the middle of next year – up from 3.2% in its last economic forecast in July. Inflation hit 3.5% in September , as measured on the consumer prices index.

items.title: Isabel Schnabel: Navigating stormy waters: reflections on monetary policy
items.body: We have moved from a world in which inflation was persistently too low to one marked by recurrent inflationary shocks; from a historically accommodative monetary policy stance to the fastest tightening cycle in the history of the ECB; and from a deeply integrated global economy to one increasingly shaped by fragmentation and geopolitical tensions. As I reach the end of my journey here at the ECB, I would like to reflect on the lessons these experiences have taught me about the conduct of monetary policy in a world that has become less predictable. My remarks today are personal reflections on how the experience of recent years has shaped my thinking about monetary policy and what it may teach us about navigating the challenges ahead. The first takeaway is that central banks should prioritise instruments that allow them to adjust monetary policy quickly as conditions change.

items.title: Is Lula’s upset win also a victory for Chinese firms in Brazil?
items.summary: With domestic profits narrowing and production capacity expanding, China’s firms are continuing to widen their overseas footprints in search of new, more lucrative markets. In this series, we examine China Inc.’s next phase of “going global” and the complex, challenging…
items.body: With domestic profits narrowing and production capacity expanding, China’s firms are continuing to widen their overseas footprints in search of new, more lucrative markets. In this series, we examine China Inc.’s next phase of “going global” and the complex, challenging international environment its companies have chosen to enter. A presidential election in Brazil, a country thousands of miles away, might seem like just another headline to many in China. But for Chinese companies doing business in South America, the stakes are considerably higher. When right-wing candidate Flavio Bolsonaro took the lead in the first round of voting in early October, Ken Liu, a Chinese exporter of digital textile printing equipment operating in Brazil, grew concerned about the implications for his business.

items.title: AI meltdown: Nvidia and Qualcomm drop more than 9%, pushing Nasdaq to worst day since April 2025
items.summary: Companies tied to the AI buildout are all selling off as concerns mount about a slowdown following the midterm elections.
items.body: Chipmakers plummeted on Thursday, with Nvidia pushing the Nasdaq to its worst day in 19 months, after this week's midterm election results raised concerns on Wall Street that the artificial intelligence buildout is poised to slow down. Neoclouds like CoreWeave tumbled for a second straight day. Qualcomm contributed to the selloff after issuing a disappointing earnings forecast for the current quarter. Qualcomm and Nvidia both dropped more than 9%, with the latter losing almost $450 billion in market cap. The Nasdaq slied 5.5%, its steepest slide since April 2025. The environment has gone from bad to worse for companies intimately tied to AI infrastructure, as the combination of rising interest rates, ballooning capital needs and the Democratic sweep in Congress has led to increased fears that wide swaths of the market are going to be weighed down by too much debt and too little revenue.

items.title: Here's what the Democratic election rout could mean for the U.S. economy
items.summary: The biggest forces shaping the economy aren't going to change just because the party in power did.
items.body: The Democratic midterm election sweep could result in changes in economic policies related to trade, spending priorities and artificial intelligence. But the biggest forces shaping the economy aren't going to change just because the party in power did. Affordability pressures , heavy levels of government spending and growth that is dependent on the artificial intelligence tail wind are likely to persist, economists say. And all of those factors pose risks to the economy. "It's in a very kind of fragile place, and I don't know that it would take a lot to push the economy off the rails, and recession becomes a much greater risk," said Mark Zandi, chief economist at Moody's Analytics.

items.title: Democratic sweep puts crypto on defensive in Washington
items.summary: Democrats in Congress could impose tougher rules on crypto and investigate President Donald Trump, ushering in a tougher era for the industry.
items.body: Democrats' sweep of Congress likely resets the political calculus for crypto, ushering in a more adversarial approach in Washington and pushing industry-friendly legislation like the Clarity Act to the back burner. With crypto critics like Sherrod Brown, D-Ohio, returning to the Senate and Sen. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., retaining significant influence over financial policy, analysts say the new Congress is likely to focus on scrutinizing President Donald Trump's personal crypto dealings over supportive industry legislation. For years, crypto fought an uphill battle in Washington, asking for clear operating rules, but often landing on the receiving end of regulation by enforcement. That shifted after Trump's 2024 election victory, giving the industry a reprieve and seat at the policy table.

items.summary: The goverment argues the change will help jobseekers and could help to prevent pay discrimination.
items.body: Businesses should publish salaries in job adverts now, the prime minister is telling firms, rather than wait for a new law to come in that will force them to do so. The government is planning to make pay details compulsory in adverts, with legislation on the issue being brought forward "as soon as possible". It argues the change will help jobseekers, particularly those applying for their first job, and could help prevent pay discrimination. However, one industry group said setting pay was a complex process and regulating adverts was not always suitable. It comes a week after the UK's equality watchdog said employees should legally be able to find out what their colleagues are earning .

items.title: Bomb threats disrupt at least 25 flights across Europe, raising hybrid war fears
items.summary: Planes forced into emergency landings or diversions two days after hoax alerts affected air travel Why have more than 30 European flights been hit by bomb threats this week? Hoax bomb threats have caused at least 25 flights across Europe to be disrupted, with some forced to make…
items.body: Hoax bomb threats have caused at least 25 flights across Europe to be disrupted, with some forced to make emergency landings, as questions mount over an apparently coordinated effort to cause chaos for travellers. The series of warnings on Thursday affected flights between Italy, Ireland, the UK, Spain, Bulgaria, Romania, Poland, Finland, Austria, Denmark, Belgium, Portugal, France, Greece, Serbia and Czechia. The threats affected flights by Ryanair, Aer Lingus, Wizz Air, Finnair, easyJet, Aegean Airlines, Iberia, Sky Express, Air Serbia and LOT Polish Airlines. All landed safely. Searches of the planes found nothing suspicious. In the UK, Heathrow, London’s principal airport, and Birmingham airport received threats overnight, but it was determined that they were hoaxes with the help of specialist investigators from the Metropolitan police’s aviation police command.

items.title: Piero Cipollone: Shaping the future of money
items.body: But to do this, it must be trusted. It must allow people and businesses to transact safely and efficiently. And it must evolve with geopolitical and technological developments. For centuries, central banks have issued money and safeguarded its value. That mandate remains unchanged. But the environment in which money is used is being transformed. People are increasingly paying digitally. Tokenisation could reorganise the financial value chain. New solutions are being considered to enhance cross-border payments. And geopolitical fragmentation is making the resilience and governance of critical infrastructure ever more important. Central banks must therefore ensure that the money they issue remains fit for the future. This does not mean replacing the private sector or predicting which technology will prevail.

items.title: What does Trump’s midterm humbling mean for Bessent ahead of talks with He Lifeng?
items.summary: As US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent prepares to sit down with Vice-Premier He Lifeng, his Chinese counterpart, in Shenzhen later this month for trade talks ahead of the Apec summit, he will do so with weakened party support at his back following the landslide victory of the…
items.body: As US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent prepares to sit down with Vice-Premier He Lifeng, his Chinese counterpart, in Shenzhen later this month for trade talks ahead of the Apec summit, he will do so with weakened party support at his back following the landslide victory of the Democrats in this week’s midterm elections. Analysts said that raised questions about Washington’s ability to deliver on any commitments reached in talks with Beijing, while potentially giving China greater leverage in the negotiations. “It’s hard for Bessent to say now that he can promise any sort of deliverable with the Chinese side when he meets He Lifeng, given that there’s great uncertainty for the Trump administration’s China policy,” said Dexter Roberts, a US-based senior fellow at the Atlantic Council think tank’s Global China Hub.

items.title: US midterms live: Nasdaq plunges 5.5% on AI regulation fears
items.body: WASHINGTON/NEW YORK -- The opposition Democratic Party has won control of the U.S. Senate and House of Representatives, according to media projections, capitalizing on widespread voter discontent over Republican President Donald Trump's policies on inflation, tariffs, AI data centers and the Iran war. In the weeks leading up to the Nov. 3 midterm elections, forecasters overwhelmingly favored the Democrats to retake the House, while the battle to regain control of the Senate was expected to be much closer. However, only hours after polls closed, Democrats flipped Republican-held Senate seats in North Carolina, South Carolina, Ohio, Texas, Kansas and Iowa, according to The Associated Press, clearing the key 51-seat threshold in the 100-seat chamber. The AP called the House for the Democrats later in the night, after the party surpassed 218 seats.

items.title: Bank of England hikes interest rate for the first time since Iran war, warns inflation will near 5%
items.summary: One policymaker voted to raise the bank's key interest rate to 4.25%.
items.body: The Bank of England announced its first interest rate hike in over three years on Thursday, raising its key rate by 25 basis points to 4%. The widely anticipated move marked the bank's first hike since Aug. 2023, and made it the last major central bank to embark on a tightening cycle since the U.S. and Israel went to war with Iran eight months ago. The majority of the bank's Monetary Policy Committee voted for the quarter-point hike, with the motion passing by 8 votes to 1. The dissenting member voted to raise the bank's key interest rate by 50 basis points to 4.25%. "The conflict in the Middle East is now in its ninth month," the MPC said in a statement Thursday. "Global energy prices have continued to rise from an already elevated level." Policymakers said they now expected U.K. inflation to rise to "about 5%" by the middle of 2027.

items.title: Nasdaq sees worst day in 18 months as investors bet on AI slowdown after Democrats’ election triumph
items.summary: Nearly $2tn shaved off Nasdaq value as worries of curbs to AI datacenters ripple across bourses The Nasdaq share index had its worst day in 18 months after slumping 5.5% on Thursday amid growing signs that the artificial intelligence industry will face tougher regulation because…
items.body: The Nasdaq share index had its worst day in 18 months after slumping 5.5% on Thursday amid growing signs that the artificial intelligence industry will face tougher regulation because of the midterm election results. As Wall Street sustained widespread losses, the Nasdaq composite tumbled into “correction territory” – more than 10% below its recent record high – with more than $2tn shaved off its value by the end of trading Thursday. The tech-heavy index had its biggest one-day fall since Donald Trump announced his “liberation day” tariffs on US trading partners in April 2025. Worries over massive AI spending gripped the New York stock market and rippled out to other bourses worldwide as investors anticipated tougher scrutiny of datacentre expansion plans. Chip stocks led the slump, with memory maker SanDisk tumbling by 22% and hard drive maker Western Digital falling by 17%.

items.title: China ready to expand US agricultural imports if Board of Trade tariff cuts take effect
items.summary: Beijing says it remains open to buying more agricultural products from the United States, but wants reciprocal tariff cuts covering US$30 billion worth of products on each side to be implemented first under the US-China Board of Trade. “China has always maintained an open…
items.body: Beijing says it remains open to buying more agricultural products from the United States, but wants reciprocal tariff cuts covering US$30 billion worth of products on each side to be implemented first under the US-China Board of Trade. “China has always maintained an open attitude towards expanding agricultural imports from the United States, provided that the agreed-upon reciprocal tariff reduction arrangement – covering $30 billion on each side – is implemented,” Huang Ling, a spokeswoman for the Ministry of Commerce, said on Thursday. The comments followed the Democratic Party’s landslide victory in this week’s US midterm elections, which analysts said could complicate trade talks between Beijing and Washington ahead of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit later this month by raising questions about the Trump administration’s ability to honour its commitments.

items.body: Flights across Europe were targeted by "hoax" bomb threats on Thursday for the second time this week, disrupting air travel across London, Dublin, and Helsinki, among others. At least 27 different flights were impacted, according to Reuters , with some forced to land unexpectedly and others escorted by fighter jets. Aer Lingus, Finnair , Wizz Air and Polish airline LOT confirmed to CNBC that some of their flights were affected. It comes after seven passenger planes across Europe, two departing from the U.K., were targeted by suspected bomb threats on Tuesday and were described as "malicious hoax threats" by the U.K. government.

items.title: Faisal Islam: How high will interest rates go?
items.summary: The BBC's economics editor views one more interest rate as likely, but thinks that will be all.
items.body: Interest rates have risen to 4% and the Bank of England has indicated there are more rises to come. The question is how many? There is a split on the rate-setting committee here. Three of the nine voting members referred to "rises" plural. One member voted for a bigger increase, to 4.25%. Three referred to just one more including governor Andrew Bailey. My read on this is that the expectation is for one more rise in February. Two and done, but it depends. It is painful for those on variable mortgages, but should not be seen as the start of a cycle of hikes. Predicting where interest rates will go is like throwing darts at a board that constantly moves around the wall, with expectations of how long the Iran War will last and its impact on the economy and prices lurching from day to day.

items.body: Debt owed by developing countries rose to a record $9.4tn (£7tn) last year, with the poorest paying the highest interest rates since the late 1980s, World Bank data shows. The UK government is preparing to champion a “new drive on debt” as part of its presidency of the G20 next year – a move the prime minister, Andy Burnham, has linked to confronting the legacy of slavery. In its annual International Debt Report, the World Bank said the rising cost of servicing external debt was preventing some governments from investing for the future. The increase in developing country debt last year, of 5.5%, was the fastest in four years, the report finds – driven by a rapid rise in private sector lending. The World Bank’s chief statistician, Haishan Fu, said: “Access to international finance has improved, but the price of that finance has not.

items.title: Three ways the interest rate rise could affect you
items.summary: Job, loans and savings are all affected by the rise in interest rates announced by the Bank of England.
items.body: Interest rates have been raised for the first time in more than three years - and it could be good and bad news for you. Rate-setters at the Bank make changes to interest rates to fulfil their role of keeping price rises at a steady level. Higher rates are meant to encourage people to spend less, reducing demand for goods and services and limiting price rises. This impacts businesses in two ways - less money to spend among their customers may mean they sell less, but also the cost of borrowing to invest as a company goes up. Many businesses, particularly small ones, have variable rate loans which are influenced by the Bank rate. Mitchell Barnes, founder and chief executive of Ryse 3D, which manufactures 3D parts for the defence and automotive sectors, said the "reality" of rising interest rates was to look at the cost of employees and people.

items.title: BT cuts almost 8,000 jobs amid sweeping cost-saving programme
items.summary: Telecoms group reports £1.1bn pre-tax profit in six months to end of September and share price touches five-year high Business live – latest updates BT has cut almost 8,000 jobs since the end of March as it pushes ahead with sweeping cost reductions across the business. The…
items.body: BT has cut almost 8,000 jobs since the end of March as it pushes ahead with sweeping cost reductions across the business. The telecoms group said its workforce had fallen by 7,731 to 90,000, excluding staff in its international business, which is being spun out in a joint venture with the US telecoms company Verizon. It had a workforce of about 130,000 people, including contractors, two years ago. Most of the cuts have been at BT’s Openreach division as the buildout of its fibre network slows, as well as through a drive to slash billions in costs by 2030. The huge cuts helped BT increase its pre-tax profit by 12% year on year to £1.1bn in the six months to the end of September. BT shares, which are listed in London, shot up by as much as 6% in early trading on Thursday, touching a five-year high and ranking it among the best performers across the FTSE 100.

items.title: China sees nearly 10% decline in marriages in 2026 so far, foreshadowing lower birth rate
items.summary: China has witnessed a nearly 10 per cent drop in the number of marriages in the first three quarters of the year, signalling a possible full-year fall in 2026 after a rebound in 2025. The country recorded 4.648 million marriage registrations in the first nine months, down…
items.body: China has witnessed a nearly 10 per cent drop in the number of marriages in the first three quarters of the year, signalling a possible full-year fall in 2026 after a rebound in 2025. The country recorded 4.648 million marriage registrations in the first nine months, down 504,000 from a year earlier, data released on Wednesday by the Ministry of Civil Affairs showed. The latest figures mean that 2026 marriage registrations would most likely see a year-on-year drop as well, said He Yafu, an independent demographer based in Guangdong province. Based on the historical share of annual marriage registrations recorded in each quarter, he estimated that nationwide marriages for the entire year would range from 5.88 million to 6.46 million couples. Even if registrations reached the upper end of that forecast, they would still be lower than the 2025 level.

items.title: Elon Musk's Tesla and SpaceX lose over $420 billion in combined market cap after midterms
items.summary: Elon Musk's Tesla and SpaceX lose $420 billion in combined market cap after midterms
items.body: SpaceX and Tesla shares declined by about 9% and 11%, respectively, on Thursday afternoon with investors concerned that Elon Musk could face new congressional probes — and his companies stricter regulation — following the U.S. midterm elections. The declines, which correlated with a broader tech sell-off , brought aggregate market cap losses for SpaceX and Tesla to over $420 billion since Tuesday's close. Musk's wealth, which had topped $1 trillion after SpaceX's initial public offering in June, is now down below $800 billion, having dropped about $90 billion in the past week, according to Forbes . He is still the richest man in the world. Musk was the biggest donor to GOP candidates and causes in the midterms, with his financial contributions exceeding $470 million , the Financial Times first reported.

items.title: Drunk and dangerous e-bike riders face on-the-spot fines under crackdown
items.summary: A consultation will consider fines and other ways to clamp down on dangerous e-bike riders.
items.body: People riding drunk or dangerously on e-bikes – and those who jump red lights - could face on-the-spot fines under plans to curb anti-social behaviour. Firms which run shared e-bike schemes will also be expected to manage their fleets better and provide designated parking areas to keep pavements safe. They could also be required to take out insurance so people can claim compensation if they are hit by someone on a shared bike. It's part of a crackdown on what ministers called the "wild west" of e-biking – with a patchwork of rules across the country often leaving the streets unsafe for pedestrians. A consultation launched on Thursday sets out proposed national standards to make journeys safer for everyone and keep pavements clear, particularly for wheelchair users and families with prams.

items.title: Poundland’s US owner says retailer remains ‘vulnerable’, after talks with ministers
items.summary: Gordon Brothers still in ‘active discussions’ with interested parties and seeking to ‘protect as many jobs as possible’ The US owner of Poundland has said the high street chain remains “challenged and vulnerable” after holding talks with ministers amid government criticism of…
items.body: The US owner of Poundland has said the high street chain remains “challenged and vulnerable” after holding talks with ministers amid government criticism of its handling of the retailer. Gordon Brothers said on Thursday morning that it was still in “active discussions” with interested suitors and had been seeking to “protect as many jobs as possible”. Poundland filed a notice to appoint administrators last week, with the fate of its 12,000 staff and about 2,000 suppliers uncertain. Gordon Brothers, the US restructuring specialist that bought Poundland last year for £1 and launched a sale process for the company at the start of September, is under pressure to accept a bid to save the retailer, which is on the brink of collapse despite receiving solvent takeover offers.

items.title: Trump's energy deals are about to face a wave of investigations by Democrats
items.summary: Democrats are certain to scrutinize the U.S. intervention in Venezuela, administration mineral deals and the cancellation of previously funded energy projects.
items.body: President Donald Trump is expected to face a wave of investigations when Democrats take control of Congress in January. His sweeping deal-making in the energy sector is likely to become a central focus. Democrats have pressed the White House for months on the legality of its intervention in Venezuela's oil sector and its cancellation of renewable energy projects funded by the Biden administration. They have raised conflict of interest concerns over numerous deals in the minerals sector. But, until now, the opposition party could do little more than send strongly worded letters to administration officials. When the next Congress convenes in January, the Democrats will wield the subpoena power that comes with committee control, giving them the authority to compel testimony and the disclosure of documents.

items.body: A second buyer has made a rescue bid for Poundland as the discount retailer teeters on the brink of collapse, with thousands of jobs at risk. London-based Xyra Group has offered to pay off half of Poundland's outstanding debts - a key sticking point in takeover talks so far - immediately. The rest would be deferred. With Poundland close to collapse, US-based owners Gordon Brothers have already rejected a rival bid from an Irish property group which would have saved its 12,000 staff. Gordon Brothers said the business has faced years of instability and "remains challenged and vulnerable". Sources familiar with the offer said Xyra is offering to immediately pay off £12.5m of an outstanding £30m loan on Poundland's books.

items.title: ‘I never understood wind’: midterms spark hope for renewables after Trump’s hostility
items.summary: Future brightens for US developers in particular after election when voters rejected Trump’s war on clean energy After years as collateral damage in Donald Trump’s war on climate action, the Democrats’ sweeping triumph in the US midterm elections has emerged as a victory for the…
items.body: After years as collateral damage in Donald Trump’s war on climate action, the Democrats’ sweeping triumph in the US midterm elections has emerged as a victory for the global renewable energy industry, too. Across the world’s financial centres the market value of renewable energy developers climbed as the election results confirmed the Republicans had lost control of the Senate and House of Representatives. For the world’s largest offshore wind developer, Ørsted , the shift in power could spell a reprieve from the White House’s assaults on the Danish company’s multibillion-dollar offshore wind investments off the north-east US coast. Ørsted’s market value jumped by almost 10% within hours of the Democratic victory, before closing almost 5% higher. The share price of other European renewables companies active in the US also climbed.

"Recent reports raise significant national security concerns regarding the PRC's access to sensitive U.S. technology and information," the GOP lawmakers wrote in a letter to Huang unveiled Thursday, using the acronym for the People's Republic of China. They are seeking information on Huang's interactions with Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, as well as Nvidia's "security protocols against foreign adversary espionage," they wrote in the brief message, which is dated Wednesday. The letter does not specify which reports it is referring to. But The New York Times reported last week that U.S.

items.title: South West Water’s failure to fix leaks ‘putting customer supplies at risk’
items.summary: With parts of region served by company in severe drought still, regulators give it six weeks to come up with action plan Repeated failures by South West Water to tackle leaks are putting customers at higher risks of losing water supplies as parts of the region remain in severe…
items.body: Repeated failures by South West Water to tackle leaks are putting customers at higher risks of losing water supplies as parts of the region remain in severe drought, regulators have said. In a warning to the privatised company that serves 1.8 million people across the south-west of England , the regulators said it had been failing to meet targets to reduce leaks and repair burst pipes for seven years. “Leakage is 18.5% above forecast … and increased since the previous year. Given the ongoing drought conditions, these shortcomings are placing customers at a greater level of risk. This is not acceptable,” said Ofwat, the Environment Agency and the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs in a letter to the company.

items.title: Russia’s ‘eastward pivot’ gains steam as Putin confirms new China border railway
items.summary: Russian President Vladimir Putin has signed into law a deal to build a second standard-gauge railway track at a key border crossing with China, as Moscow looks to accelerate its eastward pivot and boost ties with Beijing ahead of the Apec summit. According to a document posted…
items.body: Russian President Vladimir Putin has signed into law a deal to build a second standard-gauge railway track at a key border crossing with China, as Moscow looks to accelerate its eastward pivot and boost ties with Beijing ahead of the Apec summit. According to a document posted on Russia’s official legislative information portal on Monday, Putin has now signed a law ratifying the railway deal reached with Beijing during the Russian leader’s visit to China in May. The two sides have agreed to jointly construct a new track along the cross-border railway linking Zabaikalsk in southeastern Russia and Manzhouli in northern China. Crucially, the track will use the 1,435mm gauge – the world’s most widely used standard and the one adopted by China – rather than the wider 1,520mm gauge primarily used on Russia’s domestic rail network.

items.title: Chinese AI lab Moonshot turned to Europe for Nvidia Blackwell access amid U.S. China curbs, sources tell CNBC
items.summary: Moonshot AI has sought leasing agreements with neoclouds for advanced chips in Europe, as U.S. export controls restrict their import to China.
items.body: Moonshot AI, a Chinese artificial intelligence lab that the White House accused of accessing Nvidia advanced chips remotely in East Asia, has sought access to the chips through data centers in Europe, sources have told CNBC. Deals have been discussed this year for Moonshot to rent capacity from neoclouds hosting Nvidia graphics processing units, or GPUs, at facilities in Europe, four people familiar with the matter said. They asked not to be named because they were discussing private information. Nvidia's effective monopoly over the most powerful chips has made U.S. export controls a key tool in Washington's effort to preserve its advantage over China in the AI race. American AI labs such as OpenAI and Anthropic are locked in a training and pricing battle with Chinese developers, including Moonshot AI, which makes the Kimi family of models.

items.title: Welsh aviation firm AerFin bought in £475m deal
items.summary: The company, which was majority owned by a private equity firm, said it was beginning a "new chapter".
items.body: A Newport aviation company, that has grown into a global supplier of aircraft engines, parts and maintenance services, has been bought in a deal worth about £475m. Japanese firm ORIX Aviation has agreed to acquire AerFin, which employs more than 230 people and operates from sites in the UK and around the world. Founded by Bob James, AerFin has developed from a south Wales business into a global aviation aftermarket specialist. Announcing the takeover, AerFin described it as the start of a new chapter for the company. The firm - which was majority owned by a private equity company prior to the sale - buys, sells, leases and repairs aircraft, engines and components. In 2025, the company moved into a new purpose-built, 116,000 sq ft facility , external at Indurent Park in Newport. ORIX Aviation is the aircraft leasing arm of Japanese financial services giant the ORIX Group.

items.title: Ministers to target ‘wild west’ of ebikes blocking pavements
items.summary: Exclusive: Consultation led by Department for Transport will consider parking standards, fleet sizes and insurance requirements Ministers are seeking to end the “wild west” of parked ebikes blocking pavements, as they attempt to crack down on antisocial behaviour such as…
items.body: Ministers are seeking to end the “wild west” of parked ebikes blocking pavements, as they attempt to crack down on antisocial behaviour such as cyclists jumping red lights. The consultation, led by the Department for Transport , will aim to establish national standards on issues including parking, ending the current patchwork of agreements between individual bike companies and councils. While some areas enforce rules that mean shared bikes – such as those operated by Lime, Forest and Voi – can only be left in designated parking bays, elsewhere the rules are looser, prompting complaints about bikes blocking pavements, particularly for wheelchair users, people with pushchairs and those with impaired vision. It will also look at antisocial and illegal riding, for example, people jumping lights or the use of bikes by those who are underage or drunk.

items.title: Why world’s largest online shopping festival cannot get Chinese consumers spending again
items.summary: Hangzhou bank employee Xiao Na says she has no plan to buy anything during China’s ongoing Singles’ Day shopping festival, the world’s largest online retail promotion. “When I think about hunting around for things to buy just so I can use all kinds of coupons, the money I save…
items.body: Hangzhou bank employee Xiao Na says she has no plan to buy anything during China’s ongoing Singles’ Day shopping festival, the world’s largest online retail promotion. “When I think about hunting around for things to buy just so I can use all kinds of coupons, the money I save is dwarfed by what I’ve lost in the stock market,” the 37-year-old said. “Stocks are falling, home values continue to slide, and my salary isn’t going up. Keeping more cash in my pocket is the best strategy.” Consumers across China are holding back on spending during the annual shopping extravaganza as a stock market slump and a prolonged decline in property values erode household wealth, with many families making debt reduction and deleveraging greater priorities.

items.title: How the midterms could fuel the K-shaped AI trade
items.summary: U.S. midterm results could slow data center development, raising the value of existing AI capacity while increasing pressure on debt-funded neoclouds.
items.body: The U.S. midterms could widen the AI divide: tighter data center rules may reward tech giants with capacity in hand and squeeze debt-funded companies trying to catch up. Democratic victories in key gubernatorial races raised the prospect of tougher scrutiny for data center projects, adding to investor concerns about how quickly new capacity can be built and financed. In Texas, Democratic governor-elect Gina Hinojosa has proposed a statewide moratorium on new data center permits, although projects already under construction would reportedly be exempt. As the markets digested the results on Wednesday, Microsoft and Amazon each surged more than 6%, while AI infrastructure provider CoreWeave plunged around 10%. Chipmakers Micron and Nvidia fell 7% and 3.17%, respectively.

items.title: Food, fuel and taxes – can the Democrats actually make life cheaper?
items.summary: Their message on cost of living resonated with voters. Now they must show they can deliver.
items.body: Two business owners, half a country apart, want the same thing for different reasons. In Texas, Kim Hanks, who owns Tillies, a hotel, restaurant and spa business near Austin, says rising grocery and fuel costs are forcing her to raise wages for her 300 staff. "It's been such a moving target for us on affordability," she told the BBC World Service. In Indiana, Danny Reynolds, who runs Stephenson's of Elkhart, a clothing and bridalwear store, simply wants Washington to get its act together. "My hope is that we can just find some consistency, some working together," he said. "We ran on affordability, we won on affordability, and now it's our job to govern on affordability," said House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries on MS Now's Morning Joe. But here comes the difficult part. Democrats will hold Congress. Donald Trump still has the power to block their plans.

items.title: Interest rate rise in midst of cost of living crisis will leave many incredulous
items.summary: Bank’s decision goes contrary to analysis from Office for Budget Responsibility that predicts lower inflation and little impetus for wage growth Bank of England raises interest rates to 4% Business live – latest updates An interest rate rise by the Bank of England to 4% is a big…
items.body: An interest rate rise by the Bank of England to 4% is a big call when households are suffering from a second cost of living crisis in four years. Many people will be incredulous when they hear of the decision to increase the cost of borrowing by 0.25 percentage points, looking around their neighbourhood for signs of a booming economy. The official figures show the economy has proved resilient in response to the jump in oil and gas prices after the outbreak of war in Iran, but UK high streets are struggling and the underlying drivers of inflation are absent. Most households are spending to stand still, whether it is on food, energy, holidays or leisure pursuits. Businesses are in much the same position. Like households, they have absorbed significant tax rises.

items.title: Elon Musk's millions failed to deliver Republican wins in fierce midterms
items.summary: Musk spent nearly $500m in the 2026 US midterm elections, an individual election spending record.
items.body: Elon Musk spent almost $450m (£334m) – more than anyone ever has in an election cycle – to back Republican political candidates in the US midterm races. It was not enough to keep Democrats from a resounding victory . Among the most striking wins went to Democrat James Talarico, who beat Republican Ken Paxton for a US Senate seat in Texas. Musk spent at least $45m in support of Paxton, according to a BBC analysis of campaign finance data . Other races where Musk spent millions included Arizona, Michigan, Wisconsin and Minnesota. His spending continued into Monday, records show. By Tuesday night, Musk seemed to admit defeat, joking on X that his "election-interfering space lasers didn't work." The loss this week of so many Republican seats may have significant implications for Musk and his businesses.

items.title: What does the UK interest rate rise mean for homeowners and savers?
items.summary: First rate rise for more than three years leaves millions facing rise in mortgage payments Bank of England raises interest rates to 4% Business live – latest updates The Bank of England has hiked interest rates by 0.25 percentage points, taking the base rate to 4%. It is the…
items.body: The Bank of England has hiked interest rates by 0.25 percentage points, taking the base rate to 4%. It is the first rate rise for more than three years, leaving millions of households facing a sharp rise in mortgage payments. For the vast majority of borrowers the answer is no: more than 7.3m (87%) of Britain’s almost 8.5m existing residential mortgages are on a fixed rate. That means their monthly repayments will stay the same until their current deal ends. But for some, this period of calm won’t last long: if an existing deal is finishing soon, consumers could well face a payment shock. The base rate hike will immediately translate into higher borrowing costs for the 510,000 homeowners with a base-rate tracker mortgage. The rate they pay will rise in line with the Bank’s increase.

items.title: What Trump losing power over Congress means for Iran, Ukraine and foreign policy
items.summary: Democratic control of Congress could bring greater scrutiny of Trump’s handling of the Iran and Ukraine wars, while leaving him broad foreign-policy powers.
items.body: With Democrats taking control of both houses of Congress , U.S. President Donald Trump could intensify his focus on foreign policy in his final two years in office, while facing greater scrutiny over the wars in Iran and Ukraine, experts told CNBC. Democrats will have a Senate majority and won control of the House, giving them greater scope to scrutinize the administration, shape spending and challenge Trump's foreign-policy agenda. "We are going to see a president that is somewhat constrained on matters of oversight and investigation, but on foreign policy, he does still retain a lot of latitude," Laurel Rapp, director of Chatham House's U.S. and North America Programme, told CNBC's "Squawk Box Europe." Rapp said the Iran war was a "major issue" in this election cycle amid soaring fuel prices, food costs, and inflation.

items.title: Why have more than 30 European flights been hit by bomb threats this week?
items.summary: With flights disrupted, how concerned should you be about your travel plans? More than 30 planes have been subjected to security alerts or diversions this week , with at least 25 more bomb threats on Thursday disrupting civil aviation across Europe. What do we know so far, and…
items.body: More than 30 planes have been subjected to security alerts or diversions this week , with at least 25 more bomb threats on Thursday disrupting civil aviation across Europe. At least 34 flights have been disrupted this week, beginning on Monday, when a Wizz Air flight from London Luton to Sofia in Bulgaria was diverted to Budapest. Thursday’s threats affected airports in London, Birmingham, Brussels, Bucharest, Madrid, Milan, Prague, Rome, Sofia and Warsaw, among others. So far all incidents have been confirmed to be false alarms, with nothing suspicious found by relevant security authorities. There is no clear pattern of airports and airlines targeted, although a significant number have involved Italian airports as an origin or destination. Seven flights this week were to – or from the UK – and four to or from Ireland.

items.title: Democrats to probe JPMorgan's relationship with Jeffrey Epstein when they take Senate control

items.body: Senate Democrats are gearing up to investigate JPMorgan Chase 's banking relationship with the late sex offender Jeffrey Epstein once they take control of Congress early next year. Democratic staffers on the Senate Finance Committee intend to home in on how high-ranking executives at JPMorgan handled Epstein, a source familiar with the panel's thinking told CNBC on Thursday. The person spoke on condition of anonymity because the probe of the nation's biggest bank has not been announced. The Finance Committee is likely to be chaired beginning in January by Sen. Ron Wyden , an Oregon Democrat who currently is the panel's ranking member. Wyden has made clear he plans to make full use of the subpoena powers that committee majorities wield.

items.title: Australia's oldest department store David Jones folds after 188 years
items.summary: The brand's 38 physical stores and online site will continue to operate while receivers review its operations.
items.body: David Jones, Australia's oldest department store chain, has gone into voluntary administration, putting thousands of jobs at risk. It comes after years of financial struggles for the 188-year-old retailer - known locally as DJs - as customers desert traditional shops for online shopping. David Jones's physical and online stores will continue to operate while receivers FTI Consulting review the company, said voluntary administrators McGrathNicol. "David Jones is an iconic company and so many Australians have stories and memories of visiting DJ's stores," said its CEO Erica Berthold, adding the brand has a "well-developed plan" to "reset the business for the future". Berthold thanked "customers, our team members and our partners for their continued support of David Jones through this period".

items.title: Tech barons cozied up to Trump. What will they do in newly blue America?
items.summary: Democrats’ success was helped by popular anger over tech, AI and the super rich – life for billionaires could become much more difficult The photo of Silicon Valley centibillionaires at Donald Trump’s inauguration – Musk, Bezos and Zuckerberg, front row and side by side – now…
items.body: The photo of Silicon Valley centibillionaires at Donald Trump’s inauguration – Musk, Bezos and Zuckerberg, front row and side by side – now looks like a hitlist for a blue Congress hellbent on making life difficult for billionaires. The picture symbolized at the time the bending of the knee by the richest men in the world to its most powerful, a symbiosis of the ultra-rich. Already unfathomably wealthy, Silicon Valley tycoons believed a Maga-sized public shift to the right would enrich them even more. It did. For several years, while Trump seemed an everlasting kingmaker and AI’s expansion seemed unstoppable, their fortunes ballooned to values beyond comprehension. Elon Musk’s surpassed $1tn. In the harsh blue light of Tuesday’s midterms, though, going all-in on Maga seems an unwisely unhedged bet.

items.title: California’s billionaire tax faces defeat, but Democrats plan higher taxes on the wealthy
items.summary: The likely defeat of the California billionaire tax may energize Democrats in Congress to propose federal tax hikes on high earners, according to tax experts.
items.body: A version of this article appeared in CNBC's Inside Wealth newsletter, a weekly guide to the high-net-worth investor and consumer. Sign up to receive future editions, straight to your inbox. The likely defeat of the California billionaire tax may energize Democrats in Congress to propose federal tax hikes on high earners along with a potential federal wealth tax, according to tax experts. While the votes in California are still being counted, 56% of the state's voters have voted "no" on the billionaire tax while 44% voted "yes." The ballot measure requires a majority of votes for approval, so election experts say a defeat is likely. The tax, known as Proposition 40, would have imposed a one-time levy of 5% on the net worth of Californians worth over $1 billion. Two ballot measures designed as poison pills against the billionaire tax are garnering strong support.

items.title: Elon Musk’s nearly half a billion dollars in midterms spending was a flop
items.summary: The tech billionaire set spending record as he poured $446m into campaigns for failed Republican candidates Elon Musk set a record for election spending this year after pouring nearly half a billion dollars into backing Republicans in the US midterm elections . It turned out to…
items.body: Elon Musk set a record for election spending this year after pouring nearly half a billion dollars into backing Republicans in the US midterm elections . It turned out to be a poor investment. The SpaceX and Tesla CEO contributed at least $446m to Republican-aligned Super Pacs and groups over the course of the elections, specifically targeting several key Senate races in an effort to help the Trump administration retain Republican control of Congress. He outdid his own 2024 spending of nearly $290m. Yet as Democrats swept to power across the country on Tuesday night, it became clear that Musk would get nearly nothing in return for his hundreds of millions in spending. Democrats won every one of the five Senate races where Musk’s America Pac spent the most money backing Republican candidates.

items.title: Marc Lore's Wonder confidentially files for IPO
items.summary: Marc Lore's latest startup Wonder has confidentially filed for an initial public offering.
items.body: Food startup Wonder has confidentially filed for an initial public offering, the company said Thursday. Created by serial entrepreneur Marc Lore in 2018, Wonder advertises itself as "the best restaurants from across the country, all in one place," available for delivery and takeout on its vertically integrated app. Originally envisioned as a new take on food delivery through sprinter vans outfitted with mobile kitchens, Wonder has grown to roughly 170 brick-and-mortar locations throughout the U.S. Its locations serve menu items from more than two dozen "restaurants" across a variety of cuisines, some with branding from celebrity chefs. Starting Nov. 17, the company plans to introduce more dining options through Wonder Create.

items.title: How irrational are Labour’s plans for migrant workers? To find out, read the small print | Frances Ryan
items.summary: Despite the partial U-turn on care worker visas, the staff who keep the system afloat still face a hostile environment If you want to see the senselessness of Britain’s immigration debate play out in real time, look no further than the crackdown on care workers’ visas that came…
items.body: If you want to see the senselessness of Britain’s immigration debate play out in real time, look no further than the crackdown on care workers’ visas that came to a head this week . As part of its plans to force low-paid migrant workers to wait 15 years before settlement in the UK, the Home Office has been in a battle behind the scenes for the past six months to controversially include care workers in the policy. This is despite the social care system already facing critical staff shortages and the number of British citizens and immigrants taking the jobs dwindling . After a fierce backlash from health unions and Labour cabinet members, this week the home secretary, Shabana Mahmood, announced a partial U-turn : an estimated 280,000 care workers and their dependents will be exempt and allowed to apply for indefinite leave to remain (ILR) after five years.

items.title: Barkin sees interest rate hikes ahead, but at a gradual pace
items.summary: In a CNBC interview, the policymaker expressed concern over inflation and said monetary policy will need to adjust.
items.body: Richmond Federal Reserve President Thomas Barkin said Thursday that he expects the central bank will have to raise interest rates further, though he's not sure by how much or at what pace. In a CNBC interview that was part of the Richmond Fed's 2026 CFO Summit, the policymaker expressed concern over inflation and said monetary policy will need to adjust. "Unemployment's near record lows, and inflation is too high. That means the path is pretty straightforward. The question, of course, is pace," Barkin said in the talk with CNBC's Steve Liesman. "Gradual makes sense if you think there's uncertainty in the world, and if you think that there's information you're going to get in the period. And I think that's still a pace that makes sense to me," he added.

items.title: Taiwan's chipmakers shine brightest in living memory
items.body: This week, I had the chance to meet top executives from two Taiwanese memory chipmakers, Winbond Electronics and Macronix International, at what could be the brightest moment in their companies' histories amid an unprecedented global memory chip shortage. Business has rarely been better, with record earnings being reported, and gross margins of more than 70% for Macronix and Winbond in the July-September quarter. While memory giants Samsung Electronics, SK Hynix, Micron, Kioxia, and China's ChangXin Memory Technologies compete fiercely for market share and manufacturing scale in the high-end AI memory sector, Winbond and Macronix have carved out their own niches in customized products and specialized needs.

items.title: Why do veterinary fees and sausage rolls vary in price across London?
items.summary: Location is not just the only factor on why prices differ across London, as Anna O'Neill finds out.
items.body: Have you ever wondered why the same item costs more or less depending on where in London you buy it? Take a bog standard Greggs’ sausage roll for example. If you buy it in an outer London borough like Sutton, it costs £1.35. But if you buy it in central London you're likely to pay £1.60. You might have guessed that the price difference, according to Greggs, is often about location. "We use national pricing across most of our shops however, this can vary in certain locations where costs are higher than average, such as travel hubs," they told the BBC in a statement. You might think the price of a pizza at the same chain would be the same wherever in London you eat it. A Duo Romana pizza from Pizza Express costs £20.95 in Muswell Hill, north London. But three miles (5km) further north in Southgate, the same pizza at Pizza Express costs a pound more.

items.title: What Wall Street billionaires are saying about Democrats' midterm sweep
items.summary: Billionaire political spending met criticism from ... billionaires in the wake of Tuesday's blue wave election.
items.body: America's billionaires woke up Wednesday to a political reckoning — and a Wall Street rally. As Democrats celebrated a sweeping midterm victory , some of the country's wealthiest donors traded barbs over record election spending . Others warned the results could threaten the artificial intelligence boom. Wall Street, however, cheered the outcome. The Dow Jones Industrial Average soared 1,569 points, or 3%, while the S&P 500 gained 1.6% and the Nasdaq Composite rose 1.4%, as investors welcomed political gridlock , reduced uncertainty and President Donald Trump's willingness to accept the results. Virgin Group founder Richard Branson took aim at the billions spent influencing the election. "I have felt embarrassed by the billions that tech entrepreneurs and hedge fund managers have spent," Branson wrote Wednesday on LinkedIn , calling for campaign finance reform.

items.title: Channel 4 axes Married at First Sight UK after rape allegations
items.summary: Decision made in wake of two reviews ordered following two allegations of rape and one of sexual misconduct during filming Channel 4 has axed its money-spinning reality show Married at First Sight UK, after female participants made allegations of rape and sexual misconduct…
items.body: Channel 4 has axed its money-spinning reality show Married at First Sight UK, after female participants made allegations of rape and sexual misconduct during its production. The broadcaster announced the decision following two reviews ordered after two women alleged they were raped during the filming of MAFS and a third alleged she was subjected to a nonconsensual sex act. Channel 4 removed all episodes from streaming and linear services, alongside Married at First Sight UK social channels, after the allegations were aired on an edition of the BBC’s Panorama in May. The show, which had become one of Channel 4’s biggest hits, involves single people “marrying” strangers who they meet for the first time on their “wedding day”, though the marriages are not legally binding.

items.title: Banks are turning cautious on lending, according to the Fed. What it means for the economy
items.summary: The Fed’s October bank lending survey shows tighter standards for small firms and commercial real estate, while subprime borrowers face tougher credit.
items.body: U.S. banks are starting to tighten their lending standards amid growing concern over the underlying health of the economy, according to a new Federal Reserve survey. The Fed's latest Senior Loan Officer Opinion Survey on Bank Lending Practices for October, published Nov. 2, showed an uneven credit backdrop in the third quarter, with smaller businesses, riskier households and commercial property in particular facing a lending squeeze. The latest quarterly SLOOS study for October — which pulled together responses from 61 domestic banks and 18 U.S. branches of foreign lenders — covered changes in lending standards, terms and demand during the third quarter. The survey tracks banks' reported lending standards, terms and demand, not actual loan volumes, offering a snapshot of evolving credit conditions and sentiment.

items.title: Hong Kong activist Joshua Wong sentenced to 10 years for foreign collusion
items.body: TOKYO/HONG KONG -- Joshua Wong Chi-fung, one of Hong Kong's most prominent democracy activists, was sentenced to 10 years in prison on Thursday for "conspiring to collude with foreign forces," an offense under the Beijing-imposed National Security Law.

items.title: UK found to be ‘dangerously’ reliant on China for critical minerals needed for defence and AI
items.summary: Delivering net zero also at risk, say MPs as they call for centralised policy and funding for mines and diversification The UK is “dangerously” dependent on China for critical raw materials needed for the military, renewable energy infrastructure and AI, a parliamentary…
items.body: The UK is “dangerously” dependent on China for critical raw materials needed for the military, renewable energy infrastructure and AI, a parliamentary investigation has found. MPs on the business select committee called for an urgent centralised policy and the creation of a “critical minerals finance facility” to help fund rare earth and other critical mineral mines, and deploy grants, equity and debt to accelerate a diversification programme. “Critical minerals are the alpha of the new economy,” said the committee’s chair, Liam Byrne. “We cannot rearm Britain, build AI or deliver net zero unless we secure the minerals these technologies depend on. “Yet 16 years after China first weaponised its chokehold over rare earths, Britain remains dangerously exposed.” It is the second time in a week that the government’s policy on China has been criticised by Byrne’s committee.

items.title: Nationwide strikes loom as French budget is unanimously rejected by lawmakers
items.summary: The National Assembly unanimously voted against adopting the government's proposed 2027 budget.
items.body: French lawmakers rejected the government's cost-cutting budget on Wednesday evening, as the country's finances fuel widespread protests and worry bond markets. Politicians in the National Assembly — the lower house of France's parliament — voted unanimously against adopting 2027 budget plans drafted by Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu's government. The government is trying to appease France's creditors — traders in its bonds — by drastically reducing the country's deficit and convincing lawmakers to approve sweeping spending cuts. Lecornu said in September that he was targeting spending cuts worth 54 billion euros ($61.8 billion). But no one party holds a majority in the National Assembly and lawmakers across the political spectrum sit in it, making agreements on fiscal policy difficult.

items.title: China says trade barriers block tech imports, fueling its surplus
items.body: SHANGHAI -- A top Chinese official on Thursday said China is eager to import high-tech products, but trade barriers have prevented it from doing so, pushing back against criticism of the country's large trade surplus, as he presided over a trade fair.

items.title: Amtrak workers’ union denounces plan to let passengers bring guns on trains: ‘Sheer lunacy’
items.summary: New policy would permit passengers to take firearms to their seats in lockboxes on 1,500 trains a day across the US The Transport Workers Union, which represents 360 onboard service workers at the national passenger rail operator Amtrak, has lambasted the planned implementation…
items.body: The Transport Workers Union, which represents 360 onboard service workers at the national passenger rail operator Amtrak , has lambasted the planned implementation of a new policy that would permit passengers to bring their guns on its US intercity trains. The forthcoming protocols will allow people to carry on firearms in personal lock boxes. “You can’t walk on to a plane with a gun, it has to be checked with your luggage and stowed away,” said John Feltz, International Rail Division director of the Transport Workers Union (TWU), in a statement. “So why allow guns in passenger cars on trains where there are also passengers in confined spaces? This is sheer lunacy.” The union noted the new policy was now scheduled to begin in January 2027.

items.title: World's largest olive oil company plummets 20% after rivals agree to takeover deal
items.summary: The world's largest olive oil company, Deoleo, plummeted in early trading after two of its rivals announced plans to acquire the firm.
items.body: Shares of Deoleo , the world's largest olive oil company, plummeted Thursday after two rivals announced plans to acquire the company, a deal that would further consolidate Spain's dominance in the sector. Spanish olive oil firms Dcoop and Acesur will each hold a 50% stake in the company, resulting in a new olive oil giant in the region. The deal is intended to boost olive oil consumption worldwide and support farmers in creating value through the supply chain, Dcoop said in an announcement. Deoleo said in a separate statement that it has accepted the offer, which implies an enterprise value of 520 million euros ($583.2 million ). "This milestone marks the start of a new phase, built on solid foundations and with a long-term vision to continue creating value for the sector and all our stakeholders," said Deoleo CEO Cristóbal Valdés. Deoleo was last trading down 19.9%.
